=== FILE: (Do not) use this BJJ move... 😅 [SZEXJ4u-Loo].en.txt ===

The can opener is a great way to piss people off, but it is a pretty effective move. GSP use this move all the time in MMA, but if you're doing jiu-jitsu, I highly recommend against it. What it is is a neck crank where you pull their head forward. If they tap, they tap, but they can also just let go of their legs and then take the pressure off of them. It definitely can be an effective move, but just not a nice thing to do your training partners in competition. If it's allowed, maybe go for it. But in training, don't can open our

=== FILE: 1 tip to IMMEDIATELY improve your Jiu-Jitsu 💥🥋 [gvJyyVQvU70].en.txt ===

If I could give you just one tip to improve your jiu-jitsu. What I would say is make sure you don't get your back pinned to the mat. This isn't to say you can't be on your back momentarily. You need to make sure that you're able to rotate your body and get on your side as needed because this is when things go wrong. If she pins me on my back and I can't move, well, now I can't get effective jiu-jitsu going. I need to make sure I'm able to get onto my side. I'm able to rotate and start working from here. Same thing with butterfly guard. If I'm here on my butt or on my side, I can get good offense going. But if she has me pinned on my back, again, I can't move. And now it's much easier for her to pass. That could be closed guard as well. We don't want to be pinned to the our backs. But from here, if I'm pinned on my back and I can't move, well, how am I going to get offense going? If I'm able to get onto my side, I'm able to get triangles going, scissor sweeps, all these different attacks where I couldn't get if I was pinned with my back on the mat.

 3. Targets In the guard, there are many different areas where you can control the top player using your hands and feet. When it comes to your feet, there are three targets that are especially advantageous. In fact, most guards are just names for different ways you position your feet in these three target areas. These target areas are inside the elbows, the hips, and inside the knees. What this ends up looking like is as follows. The inside of the elbows, spider guard and lasso guard. With lasso guard, you use the instep of your foot in the inside of their elbow. It offers a ton of control over the top player's arms and shoulders. With spider guard, you use the flat of your foot on the inside of the elbows. This also offers a ton of control over the arms and shoulders. When it comes to your feet on the hips, this might look like holler and sleeve guard, where you grab the collar and sleeve with your hands and place your feet on the hips. Or reverse deliheva, where you place one foot on the inside of the knee and often one foot on the hip. When it comes to the inside of the knees, deliheva is a great example as is reverse deliheva. With deliheva, you use the foot of your outside leg in the inside of their knee. And with reverse deliheva, you're using the foot of your inside leg in the inside of your opponent's knee. X guard is a great example of one foot on the inside of their knee and one foot on their hip. I could go on, but I'm sure that you get the point. That the inside of the elbows, the hips and the inside of the knees are great places to position your feet. This is specifically true when your opponent is standing. When your opponent is on their knees, you're generally hooking or wrapping your leg or legs around one leg or their torso, meaning half guard or close guard, or placing your feet between their knees for something like butterfly guard. Lock a post and drive or lift and rotate. What you are doing when you're sweeping or taking someone down is either blocking a post and driving their body over it or lifting them up and rotating them. It's really that simple. It's not always easy, but conceptually it is that simple. Block and drive or lift and rotate. Combinations of both are possible too, but when you frame it like this, the objective becomes a lot more clear. Get and keep your opponent's hips on the mat. One of the major goals in grappling is to get your opponent's hips to the mat and keep them there, as well as keep your hips off the mat. Of course, in your guard you do have your hips on the mat, but one of the major goals from guard is to sweep, which is to get your hips off the mat. For sweeps, takedowns, wrestle ups, and most submissions and dominant positions, you are looking to get and keep your opponent's hips on the mat, which is why you need to prioritize doing that. You don't want to almost sweep or almost pass or almost take your opponent down, just for them to get their hips off the mat. So prioritize getting and keeping your opponent's hips on the mat, as well as getting your hips off the mat as an effective way to defend. Get your chest onto your opponent's torso. The back, for example, your chest to back, and mount side control nor self, for example, your chest to chest. And often the sooner that you get chest to torso, the better. Many takedowns, for example, you get chest to chest or chest to back, and many passes, for example, like half guard or body lock passing, you get chest to chest. Passing chest to chest is a very smashing and controlling way to pass, and usually offers less risk of scramble starting compared to outside passing where you're not chest to chest. So keep that in mind that one of the main goals in grappling is to either get chest to chest or chest to back. Connect to the upper body or the lower body, takedowns. To grapple, you need to be connected to your opponent. You can't actually grapple if you're not even touching your opponent. Maybe there's exception if you're a Jedi and you're using the force, but for us mere mortals, you need to make meaningful connections to the upper body or lower body or a combination of both. Of course, a human only has an upper and lower body, but thinking of connecting to either one makes the objectives in grappling feel a lot more simple and easier to understand. For example, takedowns. You can connect to the lower body by grabbing one leg or two legs. Grabbing one leg is a single leg and grabbing two legs is a double leg. You can also connect to the upper body using grips such as under hooks, body locks, over hooks, and you can even grab the jacket, etc. Once you've either connected to the upper body or lower body or a combination of both, now you're just looking to get your opponent's legs off the mat. You're looking to get their hips on the mat. In other areas, to just see this concept also remains true. Connect to the upper body or lower body guard. Again, you can connect to the upper body or lower body simultaneously, but generally you're going to be connected to either one or other primarily. For example, lasso and spider guard are very much upper body guards. Deliheva and reverse Deliheva are very much lower body guards. Generally, if the guard passer leads with their upper body, then upper body guards are usually more available. And if they lead with their legs, then lower body guards are usually most available. === FILE: Aim for THESE targets when playing guard! 🥋🔥 [eCez0kNQ0E0].en.txt ===

When you're playing guard, you want to think about specific targets that are available to attack. So, for example, here I could attack this near side arm. I can go for arm drags. I can go for John Wayne sweeps. Or I can go underneath the arm for under hooks, over hooks. I can attack the neck. I can start going for guillotines and stuff like that. I can attack this forearm, kamoras, shaolin sweeps, this kind of stuff. I could go under the arm on this side for reverse under hooks. I could be here in this octopus position. When it comes to these targets, there's only so many available. Again, it's this near side arm, underneath the arm, the neck, this far side arm underneath the far side arm. And when you think about it this way, it becomes a lot more clear what's available.

=== FILE: Answering Your ＂Dumb＂ BJJ Questions [l73aAR1-L-Y].en.txt ===

Your first few months jiu-jitsu can be really hard and you might have questions that you don't know the answer to. No question is dumb and I'm going to answer the most common white belt questions that white belts have that they're too embarrassed or too awkward to ask. So, let's get started. Am I too old, out of shape or unathletic for this? You're not because jiu-jitsu attracts people from all walks of life, different shapes and sizes, ages and strengths. And these people need people to grapple with too. So you training helps them out and them training helps you out. And most gyms have a good culture. So even if your physicality doesn't match with someone else's, maybe they're younger, stronger, more athletic, they're most likely going to treat you right if you're at a good gym. It's totally normal to see some 15year-old rolling just fine with some 40, 50, 60year-old because they know how to treat their training partners, right? How often should I train? In my opinion, two to three times per week is ideal for most people. When you go beyond that, that's usually for competitors or people that are just very much in love with jiu-jitsu and obsessed with it. And that can be good, but it can also lead to burnout or injuries or just overtraining in general. One time per week likely isn't enough in most cases. It's definitely better than nothing. But I think for most, two to three times per week is that sweet spot of being enough, but not too much. But it really depends on your goals, what you're looking for out of the sport. Is it normal to feel completely lost? It's completely normal to feel lost. That's probably the most common question I get from beginners is what do I do? And this is totally valid because when you start jiu-jitsu, there's so much information coming at you, so much to sort through and figure out what to focus your attention on. And that's how you get better at jiu-jitsu. You get better at focusing your attention on what actually matters. So, in the beginning, there's just so much. And when you get more advanced, it's just easier to narrow down what I want to focus my attention on. So, it's completely normal if you feel lost. How do I avoid being that guy that nobody wants to roll with? It's really not that hard. You need to basically just not stink and be a good person. Hygiene is number one. Even if you're a good person, but you stink, people will not want to train with you. And if you smell good, but you're a complainer or you hurt people or you're just someone that isn't an enjoyable role, then likely people won't want to train with you. So, it's like all things in life. Just don't stink and be a good person and people will probably want to be around you. What should I do if I'm injured or super sore? Should I still come to class? It really depends because it can be very useful to show up to class and watch class. But often times what happens is people show up to class injured and they just can't help themselves. They end up rolling and they might end up hurting themselves. This is something that's happened to me. One time I hurt my ankle really bad and I showed up to class a week later and I hurt my ankle even worse than it already was and I had to take more time off than I would have otherwise. Is it rude to ask a higher belt to roll? It's absolutely not rude to ask a higher belt to roll. But at the same time, I don't think it should be interpreted as rude for a higher belt to say no. Sometimes I just want a hard night. I want to roll with people that are going to push me and really make me work. And I always feel bad saying no. But I need to look out for my own training, too. But there's nights where I don't really care who I roll with, and I'm more than happy to roll with a brand new person. But it just depends on what I want out of that specific night. What do I do if someone's going super hard and I don't feel safe? Communication fixes most things in life. So, what you need to do is communicate with them and tell them they're going too hard. But that doesn't mean that they're going to listen. And if they don't listen, the best thing you can do is tell your coach. It's really their job to make sure that they provide a safe training environment. But it can be hard for a coach to know someone is being unsafe if nobody tells them. So, if someone is being unsafe and you tell your coach, that can also help make sure that they don't hurt somebody else and be unsafe with somebody else because other people might be too shy to tell their coach. So, really, if you can, you should tell your coach and they can deal with it. Is it okay to ask questions during class? It's absolutely okay and even encouraged. I love when people ask questions. I feel like it's so much more of a conversation and dialogue that way rather than me just doing a monologue. You're paying to learn jiu-jitsu. And if something is unclear, you should ask so that it is clear. And maybe other people have the same question you do, but they're too shy to ask. So asking can really help them. And again, most instructors appreciate questions. What do I do if I don't want to roll with someone? How do I say no? The easiest way is just to make an excuse. There's nothing wrong with a little lie just to not hurt somebody's feelings. You can just say, "Oh, I already have a partner, or I'm taking this round off," or whatever you need to do. And eventually, they're going to get the hint if you don't ever say yes. Or you can just tell them directly why. Maybe, oh, you're too big for me. I'm very small person. But obviously, be mindful of their feelings when you say no and it should be no issue. Spring is here and with spring comes change often times in the form of shifting priorities and new routines. Unfortunately, however, many feel anxiety during these transitions. For instance, all those springtime social media photos, the lofty vacations that everyone seems to be enjoying, people living their best lives. All of this content can heighten the feelings of inadequacy and fear of missing out. For example, when I was younger, I used to have that fear of missing out. Because I'm a perfectionist, I always wanted to improve, to be better than I am at the moment, and that would often lead to anxiety. Anxiety is no joke. It can be debilitating, and I know this from experience. And my paid partner, BetterHelp, can connect you with a therapist to provide support. It's easy to start. Just fill out a questionnaire and they'll connect you to a therapist who can help you. They carefully make sure that therapists on the platform are wellqualified. And their support team is there to help you if you have any questions. With over 7,000 reviews and over 4.3 rating on Trustpilot, BetterHel is a platform you can trust. Let BetterHelp rule your anxiety so that it doesn't rule you. Click the link in the description or go to betterhelp.com/jtj to get 10% off your first month of therapy. What if I fart during a roll? You basically have three options. You can own up to it and be like, "Oops, sorry about that." Two, you can just ignore it. And three, just blame it on someone else. This is probably the best way of dealing with it. You just say, "Oh man, do you smell that? I just want you to know that wasn't me." They know it wasn't them, and they think it wasn't you because they think you're not lying, and they're just going to assume that it was the people beside you. What do I do if I accidentally hurt someone? Just apologize and mean it. You don't want to just say sorry and then act like it's no big deal. They should know that you genuinely feel sorry. And you have to learn from your mistake and not make that mistake again and hurt other people the same way. For me, one time I hurt my training partner, my good friend Joey, I did a hip throw on him and his foot stayed on the mat, but his body went to the mat and he dislocated his knee. I felt so bad. But the silver lining is I learned from this. I learned to never force a hip throw and to make sure that somebody's foot comes off the mat when you're hip throwing them. And now I try to talk about that a lot. Let people know that this is a danger that can happen if you're not careful. How often should I wash my ghee? Should I wash my belt? You should wash your ghee and belt every single time you use it. Some people think that if you wash your belt, your skill leaves your belt along with it and you're not as good at jiu-jitsu because of it. But obviously that's not true. And belts can contain bacteria, all sorts of nasty stuff, all the same as a ghee. So if you're not washing your belt because you think that it's going to make you worse at tradition, maybe just start washing your belt. How do I tap if my hands are trapped? You can stomp the mat. You can say tap. And just in general, I think saying tap is the safest way of tapping. But regardless, it's your job to make sure that your training partner knows that you're tapping. So, saying tap, tapping them, hitting the mat out with your foot, whatever you need to do, you need to make it obvious. Sometimes the music is loud or you have a quiet voice like like I do. So, you can't just assume that your training partner knows you're tapping. You need to make it obvious to them to keep yourself safe.  jiu-jitsu, jiu-jitsu, jiu-jitsu, jiu-jitsu, jiu-jitsu as a whole is one big grip fight, and saying grip fighting is important is a massive understatement. Submissions are just different ways of gripping your opponent causing them to tap out. Takedowns are different ways of gripping the lower body or upper body forcing your opponent to the ground. Passes are the same, different ways of gripping the upper or lower body to stop their legs from getting in the way as you progress. If you don't understand the grip fight, you're going to have a hard time in jiu jitsu, so let's change that. We'll be looking at grip fighting more quickly as you're going to have a hard time in jiu jiu jitsu. concepts and using case studies to demonstrate the point to get you dominating on the mats by improving your grip fighting. So let's get started. The importance of grips. On the left against the big guy, I hit a fake guard pull ankle pick. On the right, I try to hit the same move, but I fail. Why? Because on the left, he had no grips to keep me away. On the right, he had a grip on my lapel, which he used to frame with his arm to keep me away so I couldn't reach him. The difference in outcome was dictated by the difference in grips. Here on the left, the passer tries to get an underhook on me, but I win the grip fight by taking an underhook on him, and I take top position as a result. The same is true here when I'm on top. The guard player is trying to get an underhook on me, but I get one on him, and I pass his guard as a result. The difference in outcome is again based on the difference in grips. Every grip needs a purpose. Here, what is the purpose of this grip? Is it to pin me down? Is it to try to submit me? Is it to show the world my nipples? Well, maybe, but I'm not sure. It looks like he's trying to use it to pull me towards him. In this specific scenario, I can't think of a reason that it would be useful, especially when he could have at least attempted to use that arm to gain head control. Here, what's the purpose of these grips on my sleeve? Are they controlling my mobility? They're not, as I can move freely, and I use my mobility to enter a better passing position. Here, my opponent is attempting to defend my rear naked choke. The purpose of these grips that he has is to relieve pressure on his neck. But is there a higher purpose, a more important purpose that he could be addressing instead? Well, if he were to fight my hands themselves, he could prevent them from locking up and fight to get my arm out from underneath his neck entirely. You only need to break grips that stop you from doing what you want to do. Not all grips are created equal for the specific scenario you're faced with. For example, here in these clips, I didn't have to break their collar grips to clear their legs with the Toriano Pass. Another good example is here. The purpose of the grips that he has on me are to break my posture. I would need to break his grips if I wanted to posture up. But instead, I decided to pass with a low posture. Although his grips were controlling me in one direction, preventing me from going up, they were also helping me go down. So no point in breaking them. Give your opponent a reason to let go. It's not like I have a bunch of Dars escapes memorized. I just fight his grips by forcing him to post. === FILE: BJJ Positions Made Simple for Beginners (Stop Feeling Lost) [xFDr4qqE2cE].txt ===

 this is a positional guide to Jujitsu for beginners. If you're not a beginner, this video will probably be boring, but if you are a beginner, you're likely to get a lot of value from it. We'll be looking at the major positions of Jujitsu, the guard, guard passing, mounts, side control, and the back. The overall objectives, common submissions available from them, tips, and more. Starting with the guard. Guard. When you're on the bottom with your legs between you and the top player, you have a guard. A guard is exactly how it sounds. It guards you from your opponent when you are on the bottom. Generally, it's much easier for your opponent to control and submit you on the bottom when you do not have a guard. As when you do not have a guard, you won't be able to use your legs to control them. Which is why they're looking to pass your guard in the first place, by getting their legs in front of your legs. Notice how in mount, side control, and the back, the attacker is in front of the bottom player's legs. In your guard, you want to use what you have available to control the top player, your legs, but also your arms. Generally, the more you can connect to the top player with your hands and feet, the easier it will be to control them. Which is why I recommend looking for four points of connection when playing guard. Three points of connection should be the minimum, but four is often ideal. You connect to the top player not just to control them and prevent them from advancing past your guard, but also to advance and position yourself. Positional advancement from your guard will either be attacking submissions from your guard, sweeping, or getting yourself behind their elbows to take the back. Sweeping means to knock the top player over to the bottom, so you can become the top player for yourself. In a tournament, you get two points for a sweep. Whether you sweep and come up on top into their guard or pass their guard as you sweep, you get two points. This is a common misconception for beginners. The top player when looking to pass will either be on their knees or on their feet. When they're on their knees, common positions for the guard include close guard where you wrap your legs around their torso, butterfly guard, where you have the insteps of your feet between the top player's legs, and half guard where the top player has one of their legs between your two legs. Common variations of half guard include half guard knee shield where you use the knee or shin of your top leg to control the distance between you and the top player. Half guard butterfly where your outside foot comes into the middle between their legs to act as a butterfly hook. When the card player is on their feet standing, there are many different types of guards and most revolve around connecting your feet to the inside of their knees, their hips, or the inside of their elbows, basically either their upper body or their lower body. Most of these guards are named after the way that you connect your feet to the top player on the inside of the knees, the hips or the inside of the elbows, which is why it's a good idea to target these areas with your feet when your opponent is standing in your guard. When you're looking to pass the guard, your number one objective should always be to stay on top. You can't pass the guard if you get swept or if your opponent simply stands up. You can't let them do either one. Of course, you also want to make sure that you don't get submitted. You need to prioritize staying on top and not getting submitted as you look to position yourself past the bottom player's legs. They will be looking to use their hands and feet to connect to you and control you. While the hands are often important to address, generally it's the feet that present the most amount of danger to you. If they can move their feet freely, they can more easily enter into submissions and enter into sweeps, which is why it's crucial to prioritize keeping the bottom players feet off of you. And this is what good guard passers do. They make sure to control the feet and not easily connect to them. You can pass on your feet or your knees, but generally I think it's a better idea to stay on your feet where you have more mobility. I love when people try to pass on their knees because it often makes my job a lot easier. A great way to think about guard passing is that you want to get past the feet first and then the knees second. In my Jujitsu theory course, I call this layers of defense. You should check that out if you want to learn more about the underlying concepts of Jujitsu. To pass, you can either go around the legs. Through the legs. Under the legs. Or over the legs. Generally around the legs and through the legs are most common. When you pass the guard, the main positions that you're looking to enter into are side control. Mount. And the back. So let's now look at those. A lot of Jujitsu practitioners obsess over a huge amount of supplements before and after training, but one of the most overlooked parts of supplementation isn't flashy at all. It's about what you put in your bottle. For a long time, I didn't think about it much either. Water was water and if I was drinking enough, then I was good. What I didn't realize is that sweat doesn't just take water with it. It also strips out minerals that your body uses to stay sharp and move well. Sodium, potassium, and sodium are the most important ingredients. Sodium, potassium, and magnesium. When those aren't replaced properly, that's when you start feeling fatigue and muscle cramps and you don't perform at your best to say the least. That's what that means to elements. A zero sugar electrolyte mix built around the minerals that your body desperately needs. No artificial sweeteners, no junk. Just the right amount of sodium, potassium, and magnesium. I'm enjoying their new sparkling cans as well as their chocolate or caramel flavors that they're perfect for winter. You can put it in coffee or drink it on its own like hot chocolate. And now you can grab a free sample pack with any order using my link so you can try their most popular flavors. Get yours at drinkelement.com slash Jordan teaches. This deal is only available through my link. You must go to drink elementy.com slash Jordan teaches. Top Mount. Mount is a position where you're on your knees with the bottom player between your knees. Typically you want to be chest to chest so you can more easily keep their back pinned to the mat. Mount is a very dominant position. In most tournaments you get four points for achieving mount and it's a great place to attack submissions. Submissions can be attacked from a low mount where your hips are closer to their hips or a high mount where your hips are closer to their shoulders. From a low mount, common submissions include the following. Americana, where you grab their wrist with one hand and your own wrist with your other hand and then rotate their arm. Arm Triangle. This is where you capture their head and arm together with your arms and then squeeze to choke them. Cross Collar Choke. This is obviously a Ghee only choke where you grab the lapel with one hand and the other lapel with the other hand to choke them. Ezekiel Choke. A bit less common than the previously mentioned submissions but for this there are both a Ghee and No Ghee version of the Ezekiel Choke. Arm Bar. For an arm bar you bring your hips to the shoulders and then throw your leg over their head and then extend their arm until they tap. Often but not always you enter S mount first, a variation of mount where you make an S shape with your legs to better control their arms as you enter into the arm bar. Triangle. Similar to an arm triangle except you use your legs to capture their arm and head rather than your arms. For the majority of these submissions you will need to separate the bottom players elbows from their body to obtain the submissions. There are different ways to do so but under hooks especially are an effective way of doing so. Separating their elbows from their body is not only a precursor to entering many submissions but it also makes it more difficult for the bottom player to escape as they won't be able to use their elbows or hands to push off of you to make space and get their legs back in front of you. Bottom Mount. The primary objectives when in the bottom of mount are position your legs back in front of the top player meaning regard or become the top player for yourself by rolling your opponent over. You need to do these while also preventing the top player from submitting you which is why it's a good idea to prioritize keeping your elbows close to your body and your hands on the top player's hips. This makes it easier to push and get your legs back in front as well as prevent many submissions from the top player. As again many submissions from the top require separating the elbows from the body. If you do things like reach up and unintentionally separate your elbow from your body you'll often just give your opponent a free submission. Side Control Top. Side control is a dominant position where you have passed the guard and are to the side of your opponent. The primary objectives are either to submit your opponent or answer into an even more dominant position like mounts or the back. Common submissions include the following. Americana. Morra which is similar to an Americana except you rotate their arm in the opposite direction with opposite grips. Arm Bar. Once control the arm is secured you typically want to spin around the head and enter into the arm bar position. Kanto Choke where you grab the lapel and step over their head to choke them. For all these submissions it's usually easier to attack the far arm rather than the one that's closest to you. The arm that's closest to you is the near side arm and it's something they may use to help escape more defense submissions. Which is why it's often a good idea to insert your knee underneath that arm or your knee over top of that arm. Personally I especially like going over top of it. This is called stapling and often it makes it easier to attack submissions because you don't have to worry about that arm getting in the way. A key objective for the bottom player is to regard by getting their legs back in front of you. To prevent this you may need to transition elsewhere at times if you feel the threat of them regarding. Two great places to transition to are knee on belly where you pin the bottom player's hips with your shin as well as north south where you change the angle of your body so that your feet face opposite directions. If you're looking to enter mounts you need to make sure that you do so carefully because otherwise they may be able to catch your leg as you try to and regard. You don't want to regress as you're trying to progress. Bottom side control. Primarily what you're looking to do is get your legs back in front of the top player, become the top player for yourself, or transition to turtle. It is very difficult to roll someone over from side control so generally trying to regard or transition to turtle are better options. The more easily be able to do so it's important to prioritize not letting your opponent connect their hands around your head and arm. This is a seatbelt grip and functions very much like a seatbelt. It controls you and makes it more difficult to escape and it separates your elbow from your body which is what is needed for many submissions from side control. Your priority when in side control or about to be put in side control should be to prevent your opponent from being able to connect their hands around your head and your arm. A good rule of thumb and juditsu as a whole is to never let someone grab your head. Back top position. The back is a position where you have your chest on your opponent's back with their hips between your knees. This is a very dominant position especially because their tools to defend or attack are positioned looking away from you, their arms and their legs, both facing away from you. Typically from the back you'll place your feet between your opponent's legs. These are called hooks and they control the hips. Alternatively you can secure a body triangle which is generally even more powerful. Although if you have short legs like I do it can be difficult to lock up depending on the size of your opponent. You can also use your legs to trap arms which often makes entering into submissions much easier. The most common submissions from the back are as follows. The rear naked choke where you make a V with your arm underneath their neck and connect your hand to your bicep or your hand to your hand. The bow narrow choke where you grab their collar with one hand and their pants with your other hand. Although other variations exist. The arm bar, this is one of my favorite submissions from the back. It's often set up using a comora grip. Rear triangle, this is where you bring your hips higher towards the shoulders and capture their arm and head with your legs. This is very much like a seat belt grip but with your legs. Although less common shoulder locks in either direction are also very effective. Back bottom, your primary objective is to get your back off your opponent's chest. You want to turn and face them. To do so, you need to fight where they're connected to you, their hands and their feet. When you break these or prevent these connections, the attacker will have less control over you. You'll have more ability to turn and face and progress your position. To defend against their submissions and control, it's often a good idea to focus on controlling the hands of the attacker. You don't want to let their arm go underneath your neck or attack other submissions, and they'll need their hands to do so. There's a lot that goes into grip fighting but one thing that may be helpful to focus on as a beginner is a 201 baseball bat style grip. This does a great job of controlling the attacker's top arm which is their choking arm and make it difficult for them not only to submit you but control you in general. This isn't the only way to defend and control the attacker's arm but I wanted to leave you with something helpful and actionable. If you've made it this far, I assume you enjoyed the video and if you did, I think you'll really benefit from and enjoy my Jiu Jitsu beginner course. In it, I go further into the objectives, I show you how to do all these effective moves and more, and I go over math safety and a whole bunch of other stuff that's important for beginners. And you can pick it up right now for $25 off by using code YouTube25 at checkout. Alright, if you're still here, please leave a comment or a fist bump and I'll see you guys next time.

=== FILE: Do THIS to defend against the Bow & Arrow Choke 🤙🥋 [x36wn6RAvwo].en.txt ===

What is a better way to defend the bone arrow choke? Is it two hands on the lower arm or one on the lower and one on the upper? === FILE: Don't fall into this trap... 🥋 [2yG4cfZ9tPI].en.txt ===

You see, the thing about jiu-jitsu is that it's often not about what's better or worse because context matters. For example, what's a better arm bar? The standard fundamental arm bar where you swing your leg over, throw your leg over the head, and then get the tap like that or the top lock where you throw your legs over the shoulders and then throw your leg over the head to get the tap. It's always contextual. What's the right technique for the right moment? And where beginners go wrong or even ignorant higher belts is thinking that one technique is better than another just because that's the version that they do or that's the version that they were taught because context matters so much. If you fall into this trap of thinking this is better than that, you might limit yourself to the possibilities when you're actually rolling.

=== FILE: EASIER way to think of takedowns! 🥋🔥 [aOd1nxRlslk].en.txt ===

A great way to think of takedowns is that you want to attach to the upper body or attach to the lower body and then work to take their legs off the mat. And so this comes back to focus on task goal. So this comes from optimal theory. And I've been raving about this stuff for a long time, but optimal stands for optimizing performance through intrinsic motivation and attention for learning. And so this is from Gabby Wolf and Rebecca Luthwaite. And the idea is very simple. The more you focus on task goal, more students focus on task goal, athletes, whatever, the better you perform, the better you learn. Makes sense. And the whole theory meshes and merges really well into ecological dynamics. They both just like make sense together. And so her idea is like there's kind of three critical areas that feed into focus on task goal or at least three that were ignored before. And so one of them is attentional cues. We talked about this. If we give someone an internal focus cue, their focus is on what body movements they're doing versus an external focus cue that focuses on the effect of the movement. They're going to have better functional outcomes with the external focus cues because the internal focus cues. If I tell you like, okay, throw a dart at the wall behind you and you know, I want you to aim a certain place. I want you to make sure you throw the dart quickly or whatever. Something about how you throw the effect you have on the dart versus I tell you, I want you to focus on flicking the wrist at the end, or I want you to focus on extending the elbow. In a way you could see that internal focus cue. That's a distraction away from the task. Yeah, that's true. You're not actually focused on the task. You're focused on how you do the task, how your body is moving as you do the task. That reduces focus on task goal. And then, you know, the theory goes that that's how it works. But what we see in the empirical evidence is however it works, people learn better with those external focus cues. That's a really good example. That makes total sense because yeah, if you're thinking about your elbow and your hand and not the target, then that's at the forefront of your mind. Yeah. That's a really good example. Yeah. And then, so we talked about expectancies. So there's other research, a whole body of things about the higher people's expectancies. Again, we're assuming there's a higher focus on task goal basically. And then that's increasing performance learning. And so some of the ways we see that. So one of my favorite studies, you have people doing a golf task. You get a bunch of random people. Okay. You're going to go into groups. In one group, we tell you, okay, so, so both groups, you have the same exact task. You got to hit the ball in that hole over there. One group, we tell you, like, if people that are good at golf, they'll hit it, let's say, within like one meter of that hole. The other group, you tell them, people that are good at golf, let's say, people that are good, they'll hit it within five meters of that hole. And so the people, when you tell them that, oh, within five meters of that hole is good, that makes them feel, they have better expectancies of what they can do relative to other people. They have the exact same task and the exact same difficulty. But when they had higher expectancies of how they could do, they did better. And the idea is that it's through, the mechanism is through an increased focus on the task, task goal. And then the other area is autonomy. So when you give autonomy supportive language of when we show a move, we could say, this is the one way to do this move. If you do, this is how you do an arm bar. If you do anything different, like, it's going to fail. This is the proper ideal thing. Or you could say, this is one way to do it. This could be a great way to do it. But, like, try exploring different things. There could be other ways, right? When you support people's autonomy and how they learn, the thing is, again, the idea is we have a higher focus on task goal. Because when you're focused on, oh, man, I have to do it that one way, you're not really focused on doing the thing. You're certainly not focused on getting an arm bar done. Yeah. === FILE: Ever been caught with this HEEL HOOK from the back？ 🤔🥋 [T4wyZj_aL3o].en.txt ===

We all know that there's an ankle lock here when you cross your feet, but there's also an ankle lock possible when your feet are uncrossed. It's important to understand this because what can happen is they might go for this and they might accidentally or even on purpose start flaring your heel upwards. And this is actually a heel hook. And it's important to be aware of this because you don't want to be getting heel hooked and be unaware of it and have damage done to your knee.

=== FILE: How To Do A Bow & Arrow Choke ｜ BJJ Fundamentals [M-tP5I6fwvs].txt ===

 the bone arrow choke is the most effective submission from the back in the gi, it is a need to know technique at every belt level. In fact, I won the majority of my competition matches by either arm bar or the bone arrow. However, the bone arrow is commonly taught from the seated position, which isn't very realistic, as it's so rare to be sitting on your butt when you have the back. You're nearly always going to be either on your underside, your oversight, or flat on your back. And entries into the bone arrow differ from each position. On top of that, there are countless variations and critical details that make the difference between finishing the choke or losing it. That's exactly what this video covers. This is an in-depth but easy to digest look at the bone arrow choke and its variations. Whether you're brand new or just want to sharpen your bone arrow game, this will give you the tools that you need. So let's get started. What is a bone arrow choke? The standard bone arrow choke is a choke from the back where you grab the lapel with one hand and the pants with your other hand. While pulling with your arms, you push with your legs. However, there are variations which look a bit different, yet have the same mechanics and the same effect. We will look at the bone arrow choke as a whole, not just the standard version, but everything. Elbow positioning Elbow positioning is the most important aspect of a bone arrow choke and any of its variations. What you need is your elbow of the choking arm behind your opponent's head. This is so you can fully take out the slack of the lapel. Think about a rope under someone's neck. When the rope is in front of the head, there is slack. When you move the rope behind the head, wrapping around the neck, the slack is now taken out. The same is true with your arm. When you initially grab the lapel with your hand, naturally your elbow will be in front of the head. When you then position your elbow behind the head, the slack is taken out and you're ready to finish the choke. This adjustment from in front of the head to behind the head is basically checkmate. Of course, the tap itself is actual checkmate, but when I have control of the lapel with my hand and get my elbow behind the head, I'm always confident that it's a done deal. It's like a hit of dopamine even, telling me the finish is near. For the bone arrow and its variations, you need to be dead set on making that adjustment from the elbow in front of the head to behind the head. And the opposite is true to defend the bone arrow. If your opponent sinks in the grip on your lapel, prioritize not letting them get their elbow behind your head. I can't let the elbow go behind my back. It's a bit... I'm sorry. I'm not afraid, you got this. Get your thumbs up! Get your thumbs up! Good! You got it! You got it! Luckily I got out of that one, but I think that he was being nice. A two on one grip is what I recommend. One hand on their lower arm and one hand on their upper arm. As two hands on the lower arm does little to prevent proper elbow positioning. Pushing the neck into the wrist. When you pull with your choking arm, it forces your wrist into your opponent's neck. This is an important part of facilitating the choke, but you also want to be forcing your opponent's neck into your wrist. It's a dual motion. This modified bone arrow called the chicken wing shows this well. I'm pulling the lapel of my right arm, forcing my wrist into his neck, while pushing his head with my left arm to force his neck. This modified bow and arrow shows this well. I'm pulling with my right arm to force my wrist into his neck, while driving my shoulder into his head to force his neck into my wrist. This clip shows the dual motion as well. The standard bone arrow also applies the two hands on their lower arm. The standard bone arrow also applies this dual motion. With any submission, you need to keep your opponents still. You need to prevent rotation. This is the reason that you grab the pants for the standard bow and arrow choke. You don't just do it because it looks cool. You do it to stop them from rotating their body away from you, which would position your elbow back in front of their head and your neck. Not too deep where you're entering rear knee choke territory, but deep enough so that when you pull out the slack and get your elbow behind the head, your wrist will be located on the side of their neck. You want where your hypothetical watch would be on the soft part of their neck. This is the hard part of the neck and this is the soft part of the neck. You can just grab the lapel, but that often won't allow for the deep grip that you have on the lapel. This is the deep grip that you want, which is why it's often a good idea to feed the lapel from one hand to the other hand. Underside vs Overside When you have the back, you have an underside and you have an oversight. The oversight is the side that your arm is over the shoulder. The underside is the side that's underneath the armpit. When you're on your underside, you can often just grab the pants and enter right into the standard bow and arrow choke. But with the oversight, things change because your leg is stuck. You want to bring your hips higher from your opponent's hips to their shoulders, but that's a difficult thing to do with their body weight trapping your leg. To deal with this, you can do a chair sit to get your hips higher up to the shoulders. For the chair sit, you remove your bottom hook so you can place your knee of that leg at the shoulders, and then sit back while securing the pant grip. With your other leg, you should bring your heel to their hip, as you ideally don't want to trap between their legs. Positioning your heel to the hip, hides your foot from them being able to trap it between their legs. Not that them trapping your foot is the end of the world, but it can be a good thing to do. You can place strain on your knee, and it doesn't give you as much control over their shoulders compared to having that leg higher up on the body. Not always can everything go as planned. If your bow and arrow choke is failing, often the arm bar is right there for the taking, as the positioning is very similar. In both positions, your hips are attached to your opponent's shoulders, and you have a 90 degree angle. If the bow and arrow choke is failing, transitioning to the arm bar is often a great option, as are other upper body submissions. === FILE: How WELL do you use your feet in BJJ？ 🤔🥋 [P6HK2ZFABoI].en.txt ===

I get told all the time that my feet are like hands. And the reason is is because I use my feet so much to connect to and control my opponent. The more you can use your feet to grip onto your opponent, the more control you'll have over them. And most people know that you want to connect to them with the flats of your feet or the insteps of your feet. But you should take this to a whole new level and really be thinking from nearly all situations. How can I use my feet to control them as much as possible? Because the feet really are the hands of the legs and they're super effective when you use them as such.

It's okay to cross your feet. There's a myth in Jujutsu that you should never cross your feet when you're attacking an arm bar. However, it's not true. There have been people who at world championship level completely broke opponents' arms with crossed feet and people who completely broke their opponents' arms with uncrossed feet. Sometimes it can be a bad idea. For example, when attacking an arm bar from the bottom, it can make it easier for the top player to stack you compared to uncrossed feet. But if you're already stacked, crossing your feet can help keep them close to you and control their posture as you work to get them on their back or break their defensive grips. Understand that there's many different ways to position your legs in an arm bar and what's more important than any specific configuration of your legs is that you achieve your objective of controlling the shoulders using your legs. Control the wrist. When attacking an arm bar, you need to control both ends of the lever. The shoulder and the wrist. Controlling both is necessary and I'm not saying that one is definitively more important than the other, but I focus on the wrist the most. It's a common jiu-jitsu adage for instructors to tell their students, make sure you throw your leg over their head before you fall back for an arm bar. The reason that you'd want to is that your leg over their head will help keep their shoulders pinned to the mat and stop them from coming up to top position. Often I'll grab a leg and fall back without my leg over their head because it can be quicker to do so. And then I'll throw my leg over their head. If I'm up against someone who's much stronger, I may need to grip their leg and throw my leg over their head to control both their shoulders and their hips. Minimize their chances of getting on top. Avoid defensive grips. By defensive grips, what I mean is the hand of the arm that you're attacking is attached to something else. Often their other hand to prevent extension of the arm that you're attacking. This can often be unavoidable and something you'll just have to deal with, which is annoying because it adds another step to the submission. Always, I'll loop in one of my arms for better control and greater ability to break their defensive grips. I'll often grip with two hands to finish but I won't look to break their grip with two hands like this. Attack at the wrist. The wrist is the end of the lever and when you target the end of the lever, you're fighting from a much more mechanically sound position. Often, this will look like looping in your inner elbow around their wrist or your hands around their wrist. Beginners often attack at their opponent's inner elbow and while this can work, it requires a lot of strength. Another tip within this tip is that the closer you position your chest to their wrist, the more you can use the strength of your whole body to break their grip rather than only the strength of your arms. Think of breaking defensive grips like a puzzle. Often, I'll use specific tried and true grip breaks to break defensive grips that I like and teach because they're effective. But first, usually, I'll look at what's in front of me and try to unravel their grips like I'm solving a puzzle. I think, how can I position their hands in the weakest position possible to hold on to each other? You need to work smarter, not harder, and prioritize using your brain to solve the puzzle rather than your muscles to smash through the puzzle. Clear a path. Typically, with arm bars, you go from their hips in your lap to their shoulder in your lap. Your opponent will be looking to block you from doing that using their arms. You need to get their arms out of the way so you can make that transfer hips to shoulder. From top position, this can look like taking an underhook or double underhooks, or even threatening a choke to encourage your opponent to clear that path for you. Wrist and armpit. Armpit grips provide more breaking power, because their wrist will be lower than your chest, compared to a standard arm bar where you have their wrist on your chest. If your opponent isn't tapping, it can be best to switch to an armpit grip. If you've ever tried to break someone's arm, you'll be surprised how much force it actually takes. In my first MMA fight, I was cranking on his arm with all my might. I heard some pops, and eventually he did tap, but he held out a while. It really surprised me how much strength it took. I know if I had his wrist in my armpit, then it would have been a catastrophic injury, with that same amount of force applied. Obviously, don't break your training partner's arms, but in MMA or high-level Jiu Jitsu, you gotta do what you gotta do. Alright, let me know what position you'd like me to cover next, and make sure to pick up my Jiu Jitsu theory course to learn more about the underlying principles of Jiu Jitsu.

The same is true in jiu-jitsu. From the back, it's even called a seat belt grip. When your hands come together around the head and the arm, but the same is true in other positions like side control, for example, when I connect around her head and her arm, my hands together, I now control her. Or even the front headlock, when I'm here around the head and the arm, it's just like a seat belt when my hands come together. and other positions too like kasakatami. No matter what position you're in, it's almost always a good idea to prevent the hands from connecting together around your head and your arm, which is why it's so important to prevent these type of grips. You can close the space off. You can go elbow to hip. You can start fighting the hands. But if she just lets me connect my seat belt around her around her head and her arm, now I've got control. You can also frame. You can use your arms to stop the head and arm control. === FILE: Jiu-Jitsu gyms do TOO MUCH kata... 😩🥋 [mGhtQjroorQ].en.txt ===

Jiu-Jitsu gyms all over the world are doing way too much kata. And you might think to yourself, well, katada is for karate, and karate often gets criticized for the amount of kata and unrepresentative training that they do. But jiu-jitsu, it's very similar when we do these pre-programmed static repetitions over and over again of the same move. Repetition does help, but you need repetition in a realistic scenario. That's the whole point of using a game is because you can be exposed to a specific scenario over and over and over again. So you get that repetition without repetition. This doesn't mean that showing someone how to do something is wrong. It just means that getting them to do it over and over and over again statically is just not a great use of time. So if you want to stop using kadas in your class then comment games to get my jiu-jitsu games

=== FILE: Many beginners DON'T KNOW this... 😫🥋 [ntBRSVL80kg].en.txt ===

Many beginners still don't seem to know this. You don't get points for side control. You get points for the pass. So, if you pass the guard into side control, you get three points for the pass. If you pass guard into mounts, you get your pass points and your mount points. === FILE: SUPER IMPORTANT Jiu-Jitsu concept! 🥋 [EKyP8s67FgM].en.txt ===

The concept of connecting your hips to your opponent's hips and shoulders is so important in jiu-jitsu. So, for example, here I have my hips connected to my partner. She's in my lap. I could go from her hips in my lap to her shoulders in my lap and that would connect my hips from her hips to her shoulders. What I mean is, right, I'm here, hips to hips, I could go hips to shoulders, and now I can attack here. So, this anchors me to her shoulders. So, if I have my hips anchored to her, now I can get the submission. The same thing in mounts. I can attack from here where I'm anchored hip to hip and go for my attacks like this or I could get hips to shoulders again anchoring myself so I'm attached to her. I can go for submissions like that. Same thing in close guard. My hips control her hips and I can start attacking her arms or whatever I want to do her neck. But I can also attach my hips to her shoulders and attack from here. So we constantly want to get our hips on their hips or our hips on their shoulders and denying them from doing the same to us. But how do we do that? We use frames. We deny inside positions. So, if I have my frame in the way, she can't connect her hips to mine cuz my frame is in the way. She gets past my frame inside position. Now she connect her hips to mine.

=== FILE: The JOHN WAYNE Sweep! 🥋 #brazilianjiujitsu #bjj #jiujitsu [Y-QSIWbvLs8].en.txt ===

use this Suite from half guard to make people feel helpless this is the John Wayne Suite what we want to do is grab their wrist and bring our hips underneath them when their weight is loaded onto our hips they feel weightless all we're going to do is we grab we either go underneath the leg or onto the hip bring our hips underneath now they fall over super nice

=== FILE: The JOHN WAYNE sweep! 🥋🔥 [vQraKr37gEw].en.txt ===

If you go for an under hook on your opponent and a over hook, one great way to use this against them is a John Wayne sweep. So, all I'm going to do is I'm going to grab their wrist or their sleeve, wherever I can get. I'm going to start bringing my hips underneath them. And now, from here, I can knock them over super easy and get to the top. It's important that you don't want to just fall to your side and try to pull them over. You want to get your hips underneath them. So, we scoot our hips underneath. Now, it's super easy to move them. Just like that.

But if I do accidentally, if I just put a little squeeze by accident, she could tap at any time, but I'm not allowed to choke her. So I'm just going to start with these three grips. And the game is, she's just trying to rid herself of these three grips. If she does, then she wins. And for me, it's just continuous. There's no way for me to win. So I'm starting here. Maybe she gets rid of this one first. Okay. And now I lost one. I'm continually trying to get that back, but maybe I lose this one too. Right. I lost that. Right. Maybe I start losing the underneath her neck. I lose that. Right. I want to continually get back to those positions. But when I have none of those, that's when I lose. So here I would have lost. Maybe we're here and she gets her chin out first. Now my objective is to get that back. I need to start getting underneath the neck. But again, maybe she frees herself that wrist ride. I need to start working to get that wrist ride back. She frees herself with that arm. I need to work to get that hook, that hook in place again. So all these three things are good and we can funnel our students into these positions without making them static drill it. Right. This wouldn't be such a productive use of time to be okay students. Let's statically drill. Let's trap the arm like this. Now let's trap this arm. Now let's slide the hand underneath the neck and now restart. Have your partner do it. That's something we can just do live and build real skill. You see, CLA isn't positional sparring. It might look like positional sparring, but the key difference is, is positional sparring is very open. It might be something like start on the back, work to get the submission, person that has their back taken, work to escape. And those aren't very clear objectives for a beginner. Whereas for a beginner, it can be a brand new person and they can understand, okay, I need to get my back off their chest to escape. Or for a brand new person, right? They, they understand, okay, I'm going to start with these grips. These are good grips. I just need to maintain these grips and get them back. That's so much easier to remember and focus on. And it's really important because a beginner especially has so many things going through their mind. It's just hard to focus on what's actually important. You see, positional sparring isn't bad. It's just something different. And in CLA, it's just less to focus on, especially for a beginner and really focus their intention, which is something really important in ecological dynamics is intention because of self-organization. And what that means is, is that basically our bodies do things based upon our intent. So for example, if you're playing a video game and you want to aim right to shoot a bad guy, you're not thinking, I need to move my fingers this way, my thumbs this way to make that happen. You have the intention and then your body just does things to make that happen. And it's the same thing in Jiu-Jitsu. If my intention is to keep my arm underneath the neck, my body's going to self-organize to make that happen. One of the big advantages of CLA is time on task, meaning you get to have a lot of time working that specific skill. So any of these games, like maybe the underhook game that we looked at earlier, I've got an underhook, she's got an overhook and we're going for Uchimata or knee tap. Well, we might not get that opportunity when we're grappling to even be in that position many times at all that night. But when we're doing it in a game, it's repeated over and over and over again, giving you constant feedback in the environment to improve. And just to be clear, I don't think that static drilling has absolutely no value. I just think it has limited value. And when you are at your gym and you have mats to go live and a willing partner to go live, using them as a grappling dummy doesn't really make the most amount of sense to me. When you're at home and you can't go live, that's a great time to learn about different techniques, how other people do things, and just gain that kind of knowledge. But when you're at the gym and you can go live, you should. All right, thank you for sticking around until the end of the video. === FILE: Traditional vs games-based approach to teaching BJJ 🥋 [Vn42u_TlF8M].en.txt ===

The traditional approach to teaching jiu-jitsu is all about giving the answers. It's an answersbased approach. And giving the answers isn't wrong, but a games-based approach is all about presenting students with problems to solve. And there's a lot of advantages of this. One, it's way more fun. And two, we want students to become problem solvers. So, while giving the answers isn't quite wrong, it's more so, do we want to base our whole practice around the answers when the answers, the problems, they always change throughout jiu-jitsu. It's very variable. And this is why so many gyms are switching to a games-based approach as opposed to the traditional approach. My gym included. And if you want to start using games for your gym, then comment the word games to get my games

=== FILE: Which stance do YOU wrestle in？ 🤔🥋 [CVsCJc9YDY0].en.txt ===

Left foot forward or right foot forward, which stance do you wrestle in? Traditionally, a left foot forward is a left-handed person's stance, and right foot forward is a right-handed person's stance, which is the exact opposite of striking where if you have left foot forward, normally you're a righty, and if you have right foot forward, normally you're a lefty. Coming from an MMA background, I'm used to wrestling with my left foot forward. But recently, I've been using my right foot forward a lot. I actually find that a lot more effective as I'm a right-handed person. So, let me know, right foot forward or left foot forward? What are you?

=== FILE: Why games are BETTER than static reps ❗️🥋 [gYSoPJA5bUk].en.txt ===

The main argument of the ecological approach isn't that it's wrong to show someone a technique, but it's more so that doing something over and over again statically isn't going to download the information to their brain like software. So statically going for the rear naked choke over and over again isn't going to build skills nearly as well as actually doing it in a live environment. So we could do this but in a live environment playing a game. So maybe we play a game where I'm trying to get underneath the neck and make a V for three seconds. One, two, three. If I do, I win. And she's trying to clear my hooks for 3 seconds. If she does, she wins. So, it's this upper body, lower body battle that's happening, this dilemma. And we're building skills simultaneously. So, I'm working on my attacks. I'm working on my maintaining my hooks. She's working on defending her neck and working on escaping the hooks. So, we're both getting something out of it, and we're still getting that repetition that's needed to build skills, but again, in a realistic environment. If you want to play more games that built real skill, comment the word games to get my games

=== FILE: ＂Just roll more＂ is BAD Jiu-Jitsu advice (for cardio)... [UcLqwDGNwBw].en.txt ===

just roll more to improve your cardio for jiu-jitsu isn't always the best advice. It can improve your cardio to some extent, but generally what you're doing is improving your efficiency by rolling more. And having an efficient engine is very helpful, but if you have a small gas tank, then it isn't going to be as helpful as having a bigger gas tank while also being more efficient. You could be really efficient and you're like a Prius, but with a really small gas tank, you're not going to get very far. And you could get beaten by people that are less efficient but have a bigger gas tank. I think I'm pretty efficient myself, but I know that if I don't do cardio on the side, my cardio is going to be pretty poor on the mats. What I find helpful is a fan bike, an echo bike, an assault bike. I like doing zone 2 training on that where it's slow and steady for 45 minutes to an hour. And also, I like doing intervals where it's highintensity training that's more geared towards anorobic fitness. When you work on your aerobic fitness and your anorobic fitness, you're going to build a very powerful gas tank to go along with your efficiency from training more jiu-jitsu. But if you only train jiu-jitsu as your main form of cardio, then you can only get so far in terms of your capacity. And what you want is efficiency and capacity.

=== FILE: ＂That technique would NEVER work＂ (it does) 🥋😮 [n2FjV8NoPLo].en.txt ===

This beautiful technique you probably think wouldn't work, but it actually works super awesome. So, all it is is a back roll from half guard. What we're going to do is we're going to redirect their arm, bringing it across our body, pushing them by their tricep, and then doing a back roll over our shoulder, and then getting up to top position. This works especially well if they're trying to drive their weight into you or grab your head. You can redirect their arm as they're doing that, taking out your knee shield. And then again, rolling through, inverting to hot position. Some people like to leave their knee shield in place, but I highly recommend against it. I find it way easier to get all their weight loaded onto your hips if you take it out. And again, now just a nice back roll to get the finish.
